processing: A clonal Anxi plant made as a rolled oolong; modern lots are often in the light, fragrant style, like other Anxi oolongs.
harvest_season: Not documented in detail; Anxi oolongs generally come in spring and autumn pickings.
appearance_dry: Rolled pellets that run larger and more oval than Tie Guan Yin.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to yellow in the light style, as is typical of fragrant Anxi oolong.
appearance_wet: Big leaves opening out from the pellets, larger than most Anxi plants.
taste_profile: Stronger and more forceful than Tie Guan Yin in the light style, and clearly different in character. Aroma studies single out this plant from its Anxi neighbours.

brewing.notes: This tea tastes strong, so start with slightly less leaf or shorter steeps than for Tie Guan Yin.

vintage_note: Like other Anxi oolongs it is usually sold by season and year, and the light style is best drunk fresh. It is often grouped under se zhong rather than sold on its own name, and can also end up sold as cheap Tie Guan Yin, so buy from a seller who names the plant.
description:
Da Ye Wulong, big-leaf oolong, is an old Anxi tea plant generally said to come from Shanping in the Changkeng area. It takes its name from its large leaf.

It grows vigorously and its shoots stay tender for a good while, which suits oolong making. Rolled, it gives pellets that are bigger and more oval than Tie Guan Yin, one of the easier ways to tell them apart.

In the cup it is stronger and more forceful than Tie Guan Yin made in the same light style. Keep steeps short, and expect a different character, not a lesser copy.

In trade it falls under se zhong, the group for Anxi oolong plants other than Tie Guan Yin. That group is also what dishonest sellers pass off as Tie Guan Yin. Honest labelling is worth more here than a fancy name.
history:
From the 1950s, China's commodity inspection bodies sorted Anxi oolong into Tie Guan Yin, se zhong and oolong for grading. Da Ye Wulong is listed among the more than fifty se zhong plants.

A story crediting a named Qing-era farmer with bringing it into cultivation circulates among sellers, but it should be taken as legend. More recently, a study of six Anxi plants found this one had the highest level of dihydrolinalool and the most distinct aroma chemistry of the group.
